query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the selected HEA, superconductivity at low temperature emerges because the high configurational entropy stabilizes a homogeneous, simple crystalline matrix (e.g., a bcc solid solution) that promotes robust electron‐phonon mediated Cooper pairing despite strong atomic disorder. Lowering the overall entropy (by partially replacing one of the constituent metals with a chemically similar but less randomly distributed element) will degrade this stabilizing effect, thereby lowering Tc and reducing the superconducting volume fraction.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy produced by mixing five (or more) transition metals in near-equiatomic ratios that crystallizes into a simple, disordered structure (e.g., a bcc solid solution) and has not yet been evaluated for superconductivity at low temperature.
generation.intervention: Modify the composition by substituting a small fraction (~10 at.%) of one transition metal with a chemically similar element that does not participate as fully in random mixing (thus reducing configurational entropy), while keeping processing conditions and phase unchanged.
generation.conditions: Measurements are performed in the low temperature regime (e.g., 2–10 K) at ambient pressure under zero applied magnetic field; structural integrity is confirmed by X-ray diffraction to ensure the retention of the bcc phase.
generation.structural_mediator: A robust, disordered but homogeneous bcc crystal lattice whose stability is maintained by high configurational entropy.
generation.mechanism: The high level of random atomic mixing minimizes detrimental local lattice distortions and preserves an electronic structure that supports strong electron–phonon coupling. This in turn enables the formation of Cooper pairs under low-temperature conditions. Reducing the entropy perturbs the local structure, weakens the electron–phonon interactions, and thus impedes the onset of superconductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline high-entropy state, the modified (lower-entropy) alloy will exhibit a reduced superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and a smaller superconducting volume fraction (as evidenced by a less sharp or diminished zero-resistance transition and diamagnetic response).
generation.baseline: The original HEA with maximum configurational entropy (full random mixing of the constituting elements) and a stable bcc structure as prepared by the standard synthesis route.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold as long as (a) the overall crystal structure (bcc solid solution) is maintained and no secondary phases form, and (b) measurements are made in the low-temperature regime (approximately 2–10 K) under ambient pressure conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the Tc reduction and the quantitative change in superconducting volume fraction are uncertain until the electronic structure and electron–phonon coupling strength are directly characterized for the selected alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline HEA with full high configurational entropy and (2) a modified HEA in which ~10 at.% of one component is replaced with a similar element to reduce entropy. Confirm by XRD that both samples maintain the same bcc structure. Perform four-probe resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements in the 2–10 K range to determine Tc and the sharpness of the superconducting transition.
measurements: Temperature-dependent electrical resistance (to detect the onset and zero-resistance state)
X-ray diffraction (to verify phase and structural homogeneity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the entropy-reduced alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant lower Tc or reduction in superconducting volume fraction (i.e., if its superconducting transition characteristics remain essentially identical to the baseline sample), then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy is governing the emergence and robustness of superconductivity in this HEA is falsified.

A sharp drop to a zero-resistance superconducting state is observed at ∼7.7 K (we define TC as the temperature where the resistance changes from a finite value to zero), consistent with the results reported in ref. . Applying a magnetic field on the sample shows that its superconducting transition temperature (TC) systematically shifts to lower temperature (Fig. 1A, Inset), as expected. Temperature-dependent constant-current magnetic susceptibility characterization was also performed for the ambient-pressure sample. As shown in Fig. 1B, a strong diamagnetic response is observed starting at 7.6 K, indicative of a bulk superconducting nature. High-pressure resistance measurements were performed for four samples that were cut from the material used as the standard for the superconductivity at ambient pressure. The electrical resistance measurements for these samples were performed between 4 and 300 K. We have studied the crystal and electronic structure and the robustness of superconducting states in a HEA-type metal telluride (MTe; M = Ag, In, Sn, Pb, Bi) under high pressure using a polycrystalline sample, and the results were compared with the pressure effects for a middle-entropy system (AgPbBiTe3) and a reference system of PbTe. PbTe exhibits a structural transition from a NaCl-type to an orthorhombic Pnma structure at low pressures, and further transitions to a CsCl-type structure at high pressures. When the superconductivity of the CsCl-type PbTe is observed, it is found that its superconducting transition temperature (Tc) decreases with pressure. In contrast, in HEA-type AgInSnPbBiTe5, Tc is almost independent of pressure, for pressures ranging from 13.0 to 35.1 GPa. In addition, the middle-entropy system, AgPbBiTe3, shows a slight decrease in Tc with pressure in the CsCl-type structure, which is intermediate trend between PbTe and AgInSnPbBiTe5. Those results suggest that the robustness of superconductivity to external pressure has been enhanced by the increase in configurational entropy of mixing at the metal (M) site in MTe.
